scenarios.prompt: Your third shot from the baseline; opponents are both at their kitchen.
scenarios.explain: From the baseline vs two players at the net, a soft third-shot drop into the kitchen buys time to move up.

scenarios.prompt: Dink rally at the kitchen — the opponent’s dink floats up and sits in your kitchen.
scenarios.explain: A ball that sits up should be attacked firmly at the bodies or the middle.

scenarios.prompt: You are in the transition zone moving forward; the opponent drives hard at your feet.
scenarios.explain: Under pace in transition, a soft reset that lands in the kitchen takes the speed off.

scenarios.prompt: Steady dink rally — nothing is sitting up; a low dink comes to your forehand.
scenarios.explain: When nothing is high, stay patient with a controlled dink to a corner or the middle.

scenarios.prompt: You get a medium ball at the kitchen, but both opponents are stuck back at their baseline.
scenarios.explain: With opponents trapped deep, drop softly into their kitchen so they must hit up from no-man’s-land.

scenarios.prompt: The opponent lobs over you at the kitchen — short enough to take with an overhead.
scenarios.explain: A reachable lob is a free overhead — smash it down firmly at the feet or the middle.

scenarios.prompt: You are returning serve from the baseline. Your partner is already up at the kitchen; the serving team is back at their baseline.
scenarios.explain: Return deep — ideally cross-court — to keep the serving team pinned at their baseline, then move up to the kitchen behind your return. A deep, diagonal return buys the most time to reach the net and gives them the toughest third shot.

scenarios.prompt: A dink comes right up the middle between you and your partner.
scenarios.explain: Communicate, take the middle ball, and dink it back softly — middles cause confusion if rushed.

scenarios.prompt: A soft, floaty ball arrives shoulder height at the net — attackable.
scenarios.explain: A shoulder-height floater is an attack — speed it up at the body or the middle.

scenarios.prompt: A comfortable, low dink lands in your kitchen; everyone is at the net.
scenarios.explain: Low and comfortable means keep dinking — change direction patiently, don’t force an attack.

scenarios.prompt: Third shot, opponents up — but the return came in low and drivable.
scenarios.explain: A low, drivable return lets you mix in a drive to a gap; a drop is still the safe alternative.

scenarios.prompt: Opponents have shifted and left a clear gap up the middle.
scenarios.explain: A middle gap invites a firm drive — it causes confusion about who takes it.

scenarios.prompt: A sharp angled dink pulls you wide and you are stretched and reaching.
scenarios.explain: Stretched and off-balance, get a soft ball back to the middle and recover — no winners from here.

scenarios.prompt: The opponent speeds one up hard at you at the net, around chest height.
scenarios.explain: A hard speed-up at the net is blocked — a firm, compact paddle redirects it down into the kitchen.

scenarios.prompt: The opponent leaves a slightly high dink to your backhand side.
scenarios.explain: A slightly high ball can be sped up with control at the body — keep it medium, not wild.

scenarios.prompt: You drove and it came back at your knees as you move through the transition zone.
scenarios.incoming: Ball back at your knees, moving up
scenarios.explain: Moving through transition, soften it into the kitchen — don’t over-hit from a low contact.

scenarios.prompt: Opponents at the net; you are at midcourt and they hit a low, hard drive.
scenarios.explain: From midcourt against a low drive, reset softly into the kitchen and earn your way to the net.

scenarios.prompt: A short, low dink lands at your forehand with a tempting angle — but it is low.
scenarios.incoming: Short, low dink at a tempting angle
scenarios.explain: Low contact means build, not blast — dink to a corner and wait for a true pop-up.

scenarios.prompt: The opponent lobs you, but it is deep and over your head — not a clean overhead.
scenarios.explain: If the lob is past your reach, let it bounce and drop/reset back — smashing a bad ball gives points away.

scenarios.prompt: Your partner sped up at the opponents, whose block pops up high — the sitter comes to you.
scenarios.incoming: Opponent’s block pops up to you
scenarios.explain: A popped-up block is a put-away — finish it down at the feet or the middle.

scenarios.prompt: A sharply angled dink lands wide, low, and short, pulling you past the sideline (an ATP chance).
scenarios.incoming: Wide, low, short — pulls you off court
scenarios.explain: Around-the-post: the ball is outside the post, so there is no net to clear — drive it hard down the open court.

scenarios.prompt: The opponent keeps dinking to the same sideline spot; you anticipate and move to the Erne position.
scenarios.incoming: Repeated dink to the same sideline
scenarios.explain: An Erne takes the ball out of the air at the sideline and attacks down — surprise plus angle wins the point.

scenarios.prompt: You are in a fast hands battle at the net; the ball comes at your chest at pace.
scenarios.incoming: Fast hands battle, ball at chest
scenarios.explain: In a hands battle, a compact block/counter at the body beats a big swing — control wins fast exchanges.

scenarios.prompt: Set at the kitchen, you face a hard drive aimed right down your line.
scenarios.explain: Block the drive firmly back into the kitchen to neutralise pace, then re-engage the dink game.

scenarios.prompt: You get a high backhand at the kitchen, but the opponents are in perfect position with no open court.
scenarios.incoming: High backhand, but no open court
scenarios.explain: No open court means a controlled speed-up at the body, not a blind smash into two ready defenders.

scenarios.prompt: The opponent’s third-shot drop lands perfectly low in your kitchen.
scenarios.incoming: A perfect drop into your kitchen
scenarios.explain: You cannot attack a great drop — dink it back and stay in the neutral kitchen exchange.

scenarios.prompt: A middle ball arrives and you are the stronger forehand poaching the middle; a gap is open.
scenarios.incoming: Middle ball, you’re the stronger forehand
scenarios.explain: Take the middle with your forehand and drive/speed-up into the open gap — decisiveness rewards the poach.

scenarios.prompt: You have been pushed off the kitchen and are scrambling at the baseline under pressure.
scenarios.explain: When scrambling and out of position, a good deep defensive lob can reset the point and buy recovery time.

scenarios.prompt: Moving in through midcourt, you get a controllable chest-high ball with a gap up the middle.
scenarios.explain: It is controllable but you are still in transition — a reset is safest; a measured drive to the gap is the aggressive option.

scenarios.prompt: A wide, low ball is just outside the post on your backhand side; it is a tough but possible ATP.
scenarios.incoming: Wide low ball — clean ATP or safe dink?
scenarios.explain: If you can get around the post, drive it down the open court; if the contact is unsure, a safe dink keeps the point alive.

scenarios.prompt: A soft ball drops down the middle at the kitchen. Which player should take it, and how?
scenarios.incoming: A soft dink splits the middle between you both
scenarios.explain: On a ball down the middle, the player whose forehand covers the center takes it — for two right-handers that is Player 1 on the left. Call it early and dink it back low.

scenarios.prompt: Player 1 is stretched wide and out of position. A ball comes to the middle. Which player should take it?
scenarios.incoming: Player 1 is pulled wide; the ball comes back to the middle
scenarios.explain: When your partner is pulled out of position, the player still in position covers the middle — here Player 2. Take it, reset softly, and give Player 1 time to recover.

bands.desc: Building the basics — keep the ball in play, learn the two-bounce rule, and get to the kitchen.
You know the shots — build consistency and move up behind your return.
Solid fundamentals — sharpen your third-shot drop, resets, and patience in dinks.
Strong shot selection — tighten decisions under pace and on big points.
Advanced decision-making — refine patterns, hands battles, and avoiding low-percentage attacks.
